Title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.
Authors: Girish K Srivastava, Priyank Shukla, Sara Crespo Millas, Yogeswaran Lokanathan
Abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

Title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
Authors: Lei He, Duo Yu, Fei Xie, Kaisheng Hou, Zhaozhao Li, Meifang Dai, Jingyi Yun, Haiyan Cao, Yang Xiao, Yueyuan Qiu, Gege Shi, Wangqian Zhang, Shuning Wang, Qiang Hao, Jieyu Zhang, Zhaowei Wang, Yingqi Zhang, Kuo Zhang, Jintao Gu, Haichen Du, Meng Li
Abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

Title: p38α MAPK integrates opposing oncogenic APC/β-catenin/TCF and GUCY2C tumor-suppressor axes in colorectal cancer.
Authors: Ariana A Entezari, Adi Caspi, Jasmine R Alvarez, Andrew E Evans, Jeffrey A Rappaport, Thomas J M Kuret, Allison S Doermann, Ramkrishna Mitra, Adam E Snook, Scott A Waldman
Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract: Sporadic colorectal cancers (CRCs) form following initiating APC mutations, inducing constitutive β-catenin/TCF signaling. Similarly, the guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C) tumor suppressor axis is universally silenced in CRC. While the GUCY2C receptor is retained, loss of its paracrine hormones guanylin (GUCA2A) and uroguanylin (GUCA2B) is among the earliest events in transformation. Mutant APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling driving CRC transcriptionally silences GUCY2C hormone expression while suppressing that oncogenic pathway reconstitutes hormone production opposing tumorigenesis. p38α opposes tumor initiation, and its loss promotes transformation in chemical and genetic mouse models of CRC. In healthy intestine, p38α supports a gradient of epithelial differentiation along the crypt-surface axis. Here, we reveal that p38α links regulation of oncogenic APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling and GUCY2C hormone expression. Regulation of p38α by APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling was defined in four genetically engineered human CRC cell lines with conditional oncogenic APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling and healthy human colon organoids. Expression of p38α was eliminated from conditional human CRC cell lines by pharmacological inhibition, RNA knockdown, and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Transcriptomic analysis of these cells by RNA sequencing defined the set of genes regulated by APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling controlled through p38α. In CRC cell lines, APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling suppressed p38α phosphorylation and activity, whereas inhibition of APC/β-catenin/TCF restored p38α signaling. In the absence of APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling, inhibiting p38α repressed GUCY2C hormone expression. Inhibiting APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling enriched phosphorylated p38α at the GUCA2A promoter. In that context, analysis of the CPTAC proteomic database revealed that phosphorylation of p38α and its upstream kinases MKK3 and MKK4 was reduced in human CRC. Finally, transcriptomic analysis revealed that p38α is a critical signaling node controlling the expression of a substantial subset of APC/β-catenin/TCF-regulated genes in human CRC cells and patient tumors. APC/β-catenin/TCF signaling inhibits p38α phosphorylation and transcriptional activity, suppressing GUCA2A and GUCA2B expression and functionally silencing the retained GUCY2C receptor. These findings identify p38α as a signaling intermediary integrating oncogenic APC/β-catenin/TCF activity to extinction of the GUCY2C tumor-suppressor axis and reveal a broader p38α-dependent component of the APC/β-catenin/TCF-regulated transcriptome.

Title: Generation of Functional Gene Knockout Melanoma Cell Lines by CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing.
Authors: Kristian M Hargadon, David Z Bushhouse, Coleman E Johnson, Corey J Willams
Abstract: Recent advances in the treatment of metastatic melanoma have emerged only from advances in our understanding of melanoma development and progression at the cellular and molecular level. Despite the impact that such advances have made on the clinical management of this cancer over the last decade, additional insights into factors that promote melanoma progression and therapeutic resistance are needed to combat this disease. CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology is a powerful tool for studying gene function in a timely and cost-effective manner, enabling the manipulation of specific DNA sequences via a targeted approach. Herein, we describe a protocol for generating functional gene knockouts in melanoma cell lines by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, and we present an example application of this protocol for the successful knockout of the Foxc2 transcription factor-encoding gene in the B16-F1 murine melanoma cell line.

Title: CAR-NK cell immunotherapy: a comprehensive review of engineering platforms, clinical applications in hematological and solid tumors.
Authors: Salma Mohamed Awadallah, NourEldin Elmesalamy, Ahmed Reda Bahr, Basant Atef, Eeman Afroz, Hank C Hill
Journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.
